entries.answer: Artificial intelligence is software that performs tasks we would normally call intelligent - recognising images, translating, writing, deciding. Modern AI is mostly machine learning: instead of hand-written rules for every case, a model is shown many examples and learns the pattern. A large language model is trained on a very large amount of text to predict what comes next, which produces broad ability and a real tendency to state plausible things that are not true.

entries.answer: A large language model predicts the most likely continuation of text, which means it is optimised to sound plausible rather than to be true. When it does not know something, the same mechanism produces a fluent, well-formed and incorrect answer - called a hallucination. It is not a bug that will be patched away; it follows from how these systems are built. Anything that matters should be checked against a real source, and the model should be treated as a useful draft rather than an authority.

patterns: is machine learning the same as ai
entries.answer: Machine learning fits a model to data by adjusting parameters until its output matches the answers, rather than having the rules written by hand. It is split by what is supervised with labelled examples, unsupervised with none, and reinforcement where the system learns from reward. The failure mode to know about is overfitting, where a model memorises its training data and then performs badly on anything new it has not seen.

patterns: how does a neural network learn
entries.answer: A neural network is a system of connected units whose strengths of connection are adjusted until its output matches the right answer, and the name is borrowed from the brain without implying it works anything like one. The units are arranged in layers: the first takes the raw input, the middle layers build up increasingly abstract features, and the last produces the answer. A network learns by comparing its wrong output to the right one and adjusting the connections slightly in the direction that would have reduced the error, repeated over very many examples, which is what training is. The layer idea is why a network can recognise a face without being told what a face is: early layers pick up edges, later ones combine them into shapes, and the last recognises the whole. The cost is that the internal representations are not designed by anyone, so a system can be accurate and still be impossible to reason about, and it can pick up a shortcut in the training data rather than the thing it appears to have learned. That is the practical reason a good dataset matters more than a complicated model.

entries.answer: OpenAI builds large language models and sells access to them through an API, with the models being the product and the API the delivery. A language model predicts the next token, which produces broad ability and a real tendency to state things plausibly and incorrectly. That is the honest framing of what these systems are, and it is why verification matters more with them than with a lookup, which cannot invent an answer.
